Learning Objectives
Assess the anatomy of the proximal femur as it relates to surgical management.
Gain familiarity with commonly used classification systems for proximal third femur fractures
and understand their relevance with regard to management.
Determine the indications and surgical treatment options for geriatric femoral neck fractures,
intertrochanteric femur fractures, and subtrochanteric femur fractures.
Analyze commonly discussed aspects of the surgical management of proximal third femur
fractures, including timing of surgical management, patient positioning, surgical approaches
and reduction techniques, and implant selection.
Review postoperative management and potential complications of proximal third femur
fractures.

Overview
This lesson reviews femoral neck fractures (in the elderly), intertrochanteric femur fractures,
and subtrochanteric femur fractures.
Together, these injuries often are collectively referred to as hip fractures.
Although anatomically similar in terms of location, the treatment principles for the
management of these injuries are distinct.
Femoral head fractures and femoral neck fractures in younger patients are not reviewed in
this lesson.
Epidemiology
Hip fractures most commonly occur in patients 70 years or older and are more common in
women; they have a major effect on quality of life in the geriatric patient population.1-3
The risk of hip fracture increases with decreasing bone mass.

Epidemiology
Intertrochanteric femur fractures account for approximately 50% of all proximal femur
fractures and are commonly encountered by all orthopaedic surgeons. Femoral neck
fractures are slightly less common and account for approximately 40% of proximal
femur fractures.4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy
Fractures of the proximal femur are distinguished by their anatomic location in relation to the
joint capsule.
The mean femoral neck-shaft angle in the adult is 130° ± 7°. Mean anteversion of the neck is
10° ± 7°.
The greater trochanter is a prominent, laterally based structure that serves as the insertion
point of the abductors. In the sagittal plane, it is relatively centered in relation to the femoral
shaft.

The piriformis fossa is a proximal and posterior landmark on the proximal femur. It is
consistently identifiable on lateral radiographs or fluoroscopy.
The calcar is a medial area of dense trabecular bone that transfers stress from the femoral
shaft to the inferior portion of the femoral neck.
The lesser trochanter is a posterior structure below the calcar onto which the iliopsoas inserts.

Anatomy
Femoral neck fractures are intracapsular. Because of the absence of a periosteal or
extraosseous blood supply and the presence of synovial fluid bathing the fracture,
secondary bone healing is unreliable. Femoral neck fractures managed via fixation are
associated with a higher risk for nonunion compared with intertrochanteric fractures.5
Intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular. Callus formation is common with these
fracture patterns, and nonunion is rare because of the absence of synovial fluid and the
presence of an abundant blood supply6 (Figure 1).

Vascular Anatomy
The medial femoral circumflex artery, a branch of the deep femoral artery, is the main blood
supply to the femoral head. This artery terminates in the posterior aspect of the extracapsular
arterial ring.7 (Resource 1)

The lateral femoral circumflex artery gives rise to the anterior aspect of the arterial ring.
The superior and inferior gluteal arteries also contribute branches to the ring.

Vascular Anatomy
The ascending cervical arteries originate from the extracapsular arterial ring and are
divided into four distinct groups based on their anatomic relationship to the femoral
neck: lateral, medial, posterior, and anterior. The lateral group of ascending branches is
the dominant group.
The ascending branches give off multiple perforator vessels to the femoral neck and
terminate in the subsynovial arterial ring located at the margin of the articular surface of
the femoral head. The lateral epiphyseal artery then penetrates the femoral head and is
believed to be the dominant blood supply to the femoral head from this system (Figure
2).

Proximal femur fractures in young patients usually are high-energy injuries

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Proximal third femur fractures in the elderly population generally result from low-energy
trauma. Frequently, the patient sustains the fracture during a fall from a standing height,
from a direct blow against the ground, or as a result of rotational torsion of the femur.
These fractures in younger individuals often result from high-energy trauma; these
patients are more likely to be critically injured and sustain multiple traumatic injuries.
Classification
Femoral Neck Fractures
Three main classification systems are used to categorize femoral neck fractures.
Garden classification8 (Figure 3)
Type I: valgus impacted, incomplete fracture
Type II: complete but nondisplaced fracture
Type III: complete, partially displaced fracture
Type IV: complete, fully displaced fracture
Pauwels classification system9 (Figure 4)
Type I: 0° to 30° from horizontal
Type II: 30° to 50° from horizontal
Type III: more than 50° from horizontal
Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification system10
31B1: subcapital fractures
31B2: transcervical fractures
31B3: basicervical fractures


Femoral Neck Fractures
The Garden classification system divides fractures into four types based on the degree of
displacement. The interobserver agreement for this classification system as originally
described is poor. Interobserver agreement increases substantially if type I and type II
fractures are combined and considered nondisplaced and if type III and type IV patterns
are combined and considered displaced. Classification in this manner also informs
treatment, especially in the geriatric patient population. Nondisplaced fracture patterns
typically are fixed, and displaced patterns are managed via arthroplasty.
Pauwels classification system divides fractures into three groups based on the angle of
the femoral neck fracture. This is most applicable in discussing high-energy, vertical
femoral neck fractures in young patients. As the number in this classification system
increases, the verticality of the fracture from the horizontal (and the amount of shear
observed at the fracture) increases.

The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification system subdivides
fractures based on the location in the femoral neck and the degree of displacement. The
femoral neck is divided into subcapital, transcervical, and basicervical regions
Intertrochanteric Femur Fractures
Evans classification system
Type I: fracture extends cranially and laterally from the lesser trochanter (standard obliquity)
Type IA: nondisplaced two-part fracture
Type IB: displaced two-part fracture
Type IC: three-part fracture with displacement of the greater trochanter
Type ID: three-part fracture with displacement of the lesser trochanter
Type IE: four-part fracture with displacement of the greater and lesser trochanters
Type II: fracture extends caudally and laterally from the lesser trochanter (reverse obliquity).

Intertrochanteric Femur Fractures
The Evans classification system divides intertrochanteric fractures into stable and
unstable fracture patterns. In this classification system, the distinction between stable
and unstable fractures is based on the integrity of the posteromedial cortex. The
distinction between stable and unstable is somewhat arbitrary and dependent on
fixation method. For example, unstable patterns may be made stable via one method of
management or remain fairly unstable via another method of management.11 The Evans
classification system also recognizes the reverse obliquity fracture pattern, which is
considered unstable.12 Other intertrochanteric fracture classification schemes, including
the Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification system, are variations
of the Evans classification system (Figure 5). No classification of intertrochanteric
fractures has gained wide acceptance, and all classification systems demonstrate
suboptimal interobserver agreement.
In general, intertrochanteric fractures are best classified along a spectrum of stability
rather than dichotomously as stable or unstable. Features that may contribute to

Subtrochanteric Femur Fractures
Russell-Taylor classification system
Type I: no extension into piriformis fossa
Type II: extension into the greater trochanter and involvement of the piriformis fossa

Subtrochanteric Femur Fractures
The Russell-Taylor classification system divides subtrochanteric fractures into four types
based on the involvement of the lesser trochanter and the piriformis fossa. Historically,
this classification system was used to determine if a fracture could be managed with the
use of a medullary nail and if proximal locking should include fixation into the femoral
head. Modern implants with reconstruction style interlocking bolts limit the usefulness
of this classification system, and the interobserver and intra-observer reliability of this
classification system are low.13 A simple description of the features of the fracture
pattern may be more useful (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Illustrations show the Russell-Taylor classification of subtrochanteric femoral
fractures. Type I fractures do not extend into the piriformis fossa. Type IA fractures do
not have comminution of the lesser trochanter. Type IB fractures have comminution of
the lesser trochanter. Type II fractures are characterized by fracture extension into the
piriformis fossa. (Adapted with permission from Russell TA, Taylor JC: Subtrochanteric
fractures of the femur, in Browner BD, Jupiter JB, Levine AM, Trafton PG, eds: Skeletal

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Evaluation/Diagnosis
On physical examination, the affected extremity usually is short and externally rotated.
Geriatric patients require a careful evaluation of medical comorbidities; co-management with a
medicine team or a multidisciplinary hip fracture service may improve patient outcomes.4,14,15
In geriatric patients, baseline functional status should be noted and may be important for
treatment decisions.
Young patients with a high-energy injury require close examination for other associated
injuries.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
The injured extremity typically is short and externally rotated. In subtrochanteric
fractures, the proximal segment may be flexed because of the pull of the iliopsoas;
however, this may be difficult to determine via a physical examination alone.
In the geriatric population, a careful evaluation of medical comorbidities should be
undertaken. The number of comorbidities is directly related to 1-year mortality.16-19 Do-
not-resuscitate/do-not-intubate status also is a predictive factor for a medical
complication and mortality.20 In these patients, preinjury functional/ambulatory status
must be noted. This information may inform treatment decisions (particularly, if
arthroplasty is selected, whether to perform total hip arthroplasty or hemiarthroplasty).

In patients with high-energy trauma, a systematic evaluation for other injuries and a
careful assessment of the injured extremity for associated fractures should be
undertaken.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs include AP pelvis radiograph and AP and lateral radiographs of the hip and
the entire femur
A traction radiograph should be considered.

Radiography
An AP view of the pelvis, an AP view of the hip, and a cross-table lateral view are
necessary for diagnosis and preoperative planning. Full-length radiographs of the entire
femur should be obtained. Even in the absence of a distal fracture, a distal implant or
considerable femoral bowing in the sagittal plane may inform treatment decisions.
A traction radiograph may facilitate a clearer understanding of the fracture pattern if
shortening and deformity make classification difficult.21 Typically, this involves manual
traction on the limb and a single AP hip radiograph. This can be obtained as a part of the
workup in the emergency room.
Computed Tomography
CT is not part of the routine workup for proximal femur fractures.
CT may be helpful in certain situations, such as for the evaluation of sagittal plane deformity or
preoperative planning.


CT scans are not routinely obtained; however, CT may be a useful adjunct for
preoperative planning in some patients. For example, axial CT scans may aid in
determining sagittal plane displacement of a femoral neck fracture (eg, femoral head
roll-off or apex anterior deformity; ( Figure 7). CT also may inform decision making with
regard to performing open reduction for some fracture patterns. For example, CT may
help determine if fracture lines are simple and amenable to direct reduction. Even in
these situations, high-quality lateral and traction AP radiographs often obviate the need
for advanced imaging studies.
In patients with a high-energy subtrochanteric fracture (or diaphyseal femur fracture), CT
may be performed as part of a protocol for identifying an ipsilateral femoral neck
fracture. Recent evidence has suggested that MRI is more accurate for this purpose;
however, MRI may not be readily available in the emergency room at all facilities.22

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be useful to detect occult fractures or stress fractures or to rule out a nondisplaced
femoral neck fracture in patients with an ipsilateral femur fracture.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Normal radiographs do not exclude a hip fracture in patients with hip pain after minor
trauma. Moderate-strength evidence supports limited MRI of the hip as the
recommended advanced imaging modality for the detection of occult femoral neck
fractures if it can be performed in the acute setting.42 Some studies have described the
routine use of MRI to rule out a nondisplaced femoral neck fracture in patients with a
high-energy ipsilateral femoral shaft fracture; however, this protocol has not yet been
widely adopted.22,24
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management typically is reserved for nonambulatory patients and patients in the
terminal stages of life.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Nonsurgical treatment typically is reserved for nonambulatory patients and patients in
the terminal stages of life.25 Even in these situations, patients may benefit from surgical
treatment for palliation and pain control.

Nondisplaced or Valgus-impacted (Stable) Fractures
These fractures typically are stabilized, often in situ, to prevent subsequent displacement.
Implant options include large-diameter (eg, 6.5 to 8.0 mm) cannulated screws or a screw/side-
plate device.
Although the term closed reduction and percutaneous pinning commonly is used to describe
this procedure, is a misnomer because reduction usually is not performed and the use of pins
for fixation is no longer common.

Nondisplaced or Valgus-impacted (Stable) Fractures
If cannulated screws are used, they should be placed in the periphery of the femoral
neck to resist shear forces.26 Typically, these screws are placed parallel to each other, in
line with the femoral neck. One screw is placed low along the calcar on an AP view and
centered in the neck on a lateral view. A second screw is placed centered or slightly
cranial on an AP view and as posterior as possible on a lateral view. The third screw is
placed cranial on an AP view and anterior on a lateral view. The posterosuperior neck is
avoided to decrease the risk of injury to the femoral head blood supply; this area of the
neck may be difficult to accurately image via fluoroscopy to determine if screws are
extra-osseous (Figure 8). The addition of a transverse screw to this construct has been
described for more vertical fracture patterns to attain fixation perpendicular to the
fracture plane; often, this is more applicable to high-energy fracture patterns in young
patients and is controversial.27-29

to prevent iatrogenic fracture displacement (rotation) during insertion of the implant

Displaced Fractures
Displaced fractures in the geriatric population are best managed via arthroplasty. This may
include hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty.35-38
Hemiarthroplasty is preferred in older, lower demand patients. No strict age cut off exists, and
this decision should be patient specific. Hemiarthroplasty is associated with a lower dislocation
rate than total hip arthroplasty.
Total hip arthroplasty may be performed in physiologically younger, more active patients.
Cemented stems are associated with a decreased risk of complications, such as intraoperative
fracture and subsidence.39
In some circumstances, surgical fixation may be selected for the treatment of a geriatric
patient. Surgical fixation is the preferred treatment option for young patients.

Displaced Fractures
Hemiarthroplasty is the most common treatment option for displaced geriatric femoral
neck fractures. A cemented implant is preferred in the hip fracture population to
decrease complication rates40 (Resource 3; Video 1). Unipolar or bipolar femoral heads
are acceptable. Hemiarthroplasty is associated with a lower dislocation rate than total
hip arthroplasty41 (Resource 4). Total hip arthroplasty may be performed in
physiologically younger, more active patients who are likely to outlive a hemiarthroplasty
or those with preexisting hip arthritis.42,43 Total hip arthroplasty performed to manage a
femoral neck fracture is associated with a higher dislocation rate than primary total hip
arthroplasty, especially in patients with neuromuscular disease (eg, Parkinson disease)
and patients with dementia.44,45 Hip arthroplasty for the management of femoral neck
fractures can be performed via a direct anterior, lateral, or posterior approach.46

Extracapsular/Basicervical Femoral Neck Fractures
Basicervical femoral neck fractures are extracapsular, have a more robust blood supply than
other femoral neck fractures, and are amenable to fixation in the geriatric population.49
Closed, percutaneous, or open reduction followed by fixation with the use of a screw/side-

Subtrochanteric Femur Fractures
Nail selection for the management of subtrochanteric femur fractures may be confusing.
The two commonly used options are reconstruction nails and cephalomedullary nails.
Cephalomedullary nails also are known as medullary hip screws. These have a large,
bulky proximal nail body, have a large-diameter hole in the body to accommodate a
cannulated lag screw, and allow for controlled collapse in line with a standard
intertrochanteric fracture line. Reconstruction nails typically have a smaller diameter
proximal body and allow for two smaller, solid interlocking bolts into the head or
transverse interlocking bolts. They are available in piriformis- or trochanteric-entry
versions.
If the fracture does not extend into the intertrochanteric region, a reconstruction nail
can be used. The smaller diameter holes for the interlocking bolts are less prone to
varus failure than the large lag screw hole of a cephalomedullary nail.65 Two points of
fixation resist the flexion deformity that typically occurs in patients with a
subtrochanteric fracture. In addition, a piriformis starting point is associated with the
advantage of a starting point in line with the femoral canal on an AP view (Figure 15).
This is advantageous because the proximal geometry of a piriformis nail more closely
matches native anatomy, and they are inserted on-axis with the shaft. This will not cause
fracture displacement on insertion if the distal end of the nail engages the isthmus
(Table 1).

shortening and controlled collapse. Postoperative management should focus on early
mobilization of the patient and minimization of complications,96 such as DVT,
disorientation, bowel or bladder irregularities, and pressure wounds.97-99
Antibiotic prophylaxis should be administered within 1 hour of surgery and continued
for 24 hours postoperatively to prevent postoperative wound infection.
The risk of DVT is high among patients who sustain a proximal femur fracture.
Mechanical devices and chemical prophylaxis should be used to prevent DVT.100 The risk
of DVT is substantially reduced with prophylaxis; however, the exact type and duration of
prophylaxis remain controversial. Enoxaparin, aspirin, or novel oral anticoagulants may
be used.101,102 Some evidence suggests that warfarin is less effective than
enoxaparin.103

osteotomy at the level of the lesser trochanter104 (Figure 23).
In geriatric patients, femoral neck nonunion may be managed via a valgus-producing
osteotomy or, more commonly, arthroplasty.105

Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head
In patients with a nondisplaced femoral neck fracture, the incidence of osteonecrosis may be
as high as 15%. In patients with an appropriately fixed displaced fracture (Garden type III or IV),
the rate of osteonecrosis ranges from 20% to 30%.

Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head
Osteonecrosis alone is not necessarily of clinical importance unless late segmental
collapse occurs. Segmental collapse may be observed as early as 6 to 9 months
postinjury but is most likely to be recognized in the second postoperative year. In most
patients, it can be excluded after the third postoperative year.
In geriatric patients, this complication is minimized with the use of arthroplasty to
manage displaced fractures107 (Resource 11).
Arthroplasty Complications
Arthroplasty after fracture may fail because of instability, infection, loosening, or
periprosthetic fracture.

Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head
Arthroplasty after fracture may fail for reasons similar to those after primary hip
arthroplasty. Hemiarthroplasty may fail because of acetabular erosion108 (Resource 12).
Total hip arthroplasty performed to manage a femoral neck fracture is associated with a
higher risk of instability and other complications compared with total hip arthroplasty to
manage arthritis.109-112 Intraoperative fracture may occur and must be recognized and
managed113 (Resource 13).
